stories.headline: AUGUST CPI COMES IN HOT, FED HIKE ODDS JUMP TO 90%
stories.body: The August CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.4% year-over-year, matching headline estimates, but core CPI (ex-food and energy) climbed 0.3%, slightly above forecast. CME FedWatch now prices roughly a 90% probability of a quarter-point hike at next week's FOMC meeting, up from about 70% before the report.
stories.explain: Core CPI strips out volatile food and energy prices to isolate underlying, stickier inflation trends, so a hotter-than-expected core print tells the Fed that price pressure isn't just a passthrough from oil or food shocks. Markets price rate decisions off the fed funds futures curve, and a small miss on core can swing implied probabilities sharply when the market was already split. That's why a beat of just a tenth of a point moved hike odds by 20 percentage points in a single session.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD CLIMBS TO 4.97%, WITHIN STRIKING DISTANCE OF 5%
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.97%, its highest level since 2023, capping a week in which it climbed nearly 20 basis points amid a broader global bond selloff. Today's CPI print added roughly 3 basis points on top of Thursday's 11-basis-point jump triggered by a hot PPI reading.
stories.explain: Long-term yields reflect both the expected path of short-term rates and a term premium investors demand for holding duration risk over a longer horizon, and both components have been rising together this week as hike odds increase and investors demand more compensation for holding bonds through a period of resurgent inflation. A 10-year yield near 5% directly raises the discount rate used to value future corporate cash flows, which is why equity investors watch this level as a valuation ceiling for the broader market, not just a bond-market curiosity.

stories.headline: OIL EASES OFF $104 HIGH AS IRAN SIGNALS HORMUZ DIPLOMACY
stories.body: WTI crude fell 3.13% to roughly $100 a barrel Friday after touching a spring high near $104 on Thursday, as Iranian state media said Tehran would meet Gulf states in Oman to discuss the Strait of Hormuz. Even with the pullback, WTI is still up 9.4% for the week amid the broader escalation in the region.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil supply, so even a diplomatic signal that transit risk might ease can knock several dollars off the price without any actual barrel of oil changing hands — markets are pricing the probability of disruption, not just current flows. That same risk premium is why the weekly gain of 9.4% persists even after Friday's retreat: traders are unwilling to fully unwind the hedge until the underlying tension is resolved, not just talked about.

stories.headline: STOCKS SNAP FOUR-DAY SKID DESPITE HAWKISH SETUP
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.86% to 7,657 and the Nasdaq-100 gained 0.91% to 29,368, both halting a four-session losing streak, as easing oil prices offset a CPI report that all but locked in a Fed rate hike next week. Gold still added 1.04% to $4,390 even as the dollar index dipped 0.05% to 99.10.
stories.explain: A rate hike that is fully priced in before it happens tends to do less damage to risk assets than a surprise, because markets have already spent the days beforehand repricing valuations and positioning around it — the CPI report mostly confirmed what Thursday's PPI print had already signaled. That's why stocks could rally on a day when hike odds jumped to 90%: the marginal news was the retreat in oil, not the inflation data itself, since the oil move directly changes the outlook for both consumer spending and future inflation prints.

stories.headline: ORACLE JUMPS AS CLOUD REVENUE SURGES 62%, GUIDANCE RAISED
stories.body: Oracle reported fiscal Q1 adjusted EPS of $1.92 on revenue of $19.35 billion, both ahead of Street estimates, as cloud infrastructure revenue soared 62% to $11.61 billion. The company raised its full-year EPS guidance to $8.10 and its revenue outlook to roughly $90 billion, sending shares sharply higher.
stories.explain: Oracle's cloud infrastructure backlog is one of the market's cleanest proxies for hyperscaler AI capital spending, so a 62% growth rate combined with raised full-year guidance reassures investors that enterprise AI demand is durable rather than front-loaded. That reassurance matters more on a day when macro data (hot CPI, near-5% yields) would otherwise argue for compressing high-multiple growth stocks, showing how a strong idiosyncratic result can decouple a single name from top-down macro pressure.

stories.headline: ARIZONA LANDS CLEMSON GRAD TRANSFER RJ GODFREY AHEAD OF 2026-27 SEASON
stories.body: Arizona added grad transfer forward RJ Godfrey, who averaged 12.0 points and 5.3 rebounds while shooting better than 61% from the field for Clemson last season. The 6-foot-8 forward slots in as an experienced frontcourt piece for the Wildcats as the offseason roster shuffle continues, months after Michigan cut down the nets as national champions.

stories.headline: GRIZZLIES SEND JA MORANT TO TRAIL BLAZERS IN OFFSEASON BLOCKBUSTER
stories.body: Memphis traded two-time All-Star Ja Morant to Portland for Jerami Grant and Kris Murray, ending Morant's run as the only NBA franchise he'd known since being drafted No. 2 in 2019. It's the third star the Grizzlies have moved on from since their first-round sweep by Oklahoma City in the 2025 playoffs, following earlier exits by Desmond Bane and Jaren Jackson Jr.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS TURN TO DREW LOCK AS SAM DARNOLD'S HIP INJURY SIDELINES HIM FOR WEEK 2
stories.body: Sam Darnold is expected to miss Sunday's game at Arizona after exiting Seattle's 13-10 Week 1 win over New England on a hip injury suffered on a sack, though coach Mike Macdonald said the team avoided a serious long-term issue. Drew Lock, who went 16-of-22 for 187 yards and a touchdown in relief, gets the start at the Cardinals on Sept. 20.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN STUNS NO. 11 OKLAHOMA 17-10 AS NO. 1 OHIO STATE-NO. 4 TEXAS LOOMS TONIGHT
stories.body: Unranked Michigan's defense intercepted Oklahoma QB John Mateer and set up the game-winning score in a 17-10 upset at the Big House, the first loss by a ranked team to an unranked opponent this season. It sets the stage for tonight's marquee Week 2 matchup as No. 1 Ohio State visits No. 4 Texas at 7:30 PM ET, with Arch Manning and Julian Sayin headlining a game ESPN's College GameDay traveled to Austin for.

sports.detail: No. 19 Washington hosted Utah State Saturday afternoon at Husky Stadium; the Huskies started sluggish on offense and it was a one-score game at halftime after a big Utah State play. Final score wasn't available at publication time. Next: hosts Eastern Washington, Saturday, Sept. 19.

Added Texas Tech transfer LeJuan Watts (11.8 ppg, 6.0 reb last season) and Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno as Danny Sprinkle continues the roster rebuild; returning forward Nikola Dzepina just led Serbia's national team to a fifth-place finish over the summer.

Opened 1-0 with a 13-10 win over the Patriots, but starter Sam Darnold will miss Sunday's game at Arizona (Sept. 20) with a hip injury; coach Mike Macdonald said the team avoided a long-term issue. Drew Lock starts in his place.

Contract talks with restricted free agent center Jalen Duren remain stalled with roughly three weeks left before his $9.6M qualifying-offer deadline; Detroit's latest offer is in the five-year, $190M range while Duren is seeking an AAV north of $40M.

Sit six games back in the wild-card race and are 29-44 on the road; Julio Rodríguez (21 HR, 20 SB) and Dominic Canzone (21 HR, 66 RBI) lead the offense. Reliever Matt Brash's season is over. Tonight: at Athletics, Bryan Woo vs. Gage Jump.

watchlist: FOMC rate decision Tuesday-Wednesday, Sept. 15-16 — CME FedWatch now prices ~59% odds of a 25bp hike
No. 1 Ohio State at No. 4 Texas — tonight, 7:30 PM ET / 5:30 PM MT, ABC
Mariners at Athletics — tonight, Bryan Woo vs. Gage Jump, Sutter Health Park
Seahawks at Cardinals — Sunday, Sept. 20, Drew Lock's first start with Darnold out
Huskies host Eastern Washington — Saturday, Sept. 19, Husky Stadium

deepDive.title: Why Central Banks Are Bringing Their Gold Back Home
content: Buried under today's CPI and yield headlines is a quieter story with real staying power: the Dutch central bank confirmed it shifted roughly 86 tons of gold out of vaults in the U.S. and Canada to London between March and August, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest." It's a small move in tonnage terms, but it lands while gold is holding near $4,366 an ounce, up almost half a percent today, and it points to a structural buyer of gold that has nothing to do with this week's Fed odds or bond yields — sovereign reserve managers repositioning for a world where they no longer assume old custodial arrangements are risk-free.

Central banks have historically kept only part of their gold reserves at home, storing the rest in trusted foreign vaults like the New York Fed, the Bank of England, or the Banque de France — a legacy of the Bretton Woods era, when gold held abroad could be more easily used to settle international obligations or convert into dollars. The gold usually stays "allocated," meaning specific bars are earmarked to the owning country rather than commingled, but the country storing it still controls physical access. That distinction between legal ownership and physical custody is exactly what's now being reconsidered: owning the gold means little if you can't get to it, or move it, when you need to.

The playbook for this concern is well established. Germany spent 2013 to 2017 repatriating more than 300 tons of gold from the New York Fed and the Banque de France back to Frankfurt after a public audit controversy raised doubts about whether its bars were really where records said they were. But the sharper wake-up call was 2022, when the U.S. and its allies froze roughly $300 billion of Russia's central bank reserves in response to the invasion of Ukraine — assets Moscow had assumed were safely parked abroad. That single event told every other reserve manager watching that foreign-held assets, gold included, carry a political risk that doesn't show up in any yield or credit rating.

That's the mechanism connecting today's Dutch headline to the gold price sitting on this brief's market strip: central-bank gold buying has become a structural, not speculative, source of demand over the past few years, and repatriation moves like this one are a symptom of the same trend rather than a one-off. It matters for positioning because this kind of buyer doesn't care about the Fed's rate path or this week's 10-year yield move — they're not chasing returns, they're de-risking custody. For a portfolio, that means part of gold's current bid is effectively insulated from the usual macro drivers, which is worth remembering the next time gold rallies on a day when rising real yields would normally argue against it.
